blocks.title: What is this file?
blocks.what: A ServiceAccount is an identity for Pods. It comes from the core v1 API.
blocks.why: EKS Pod Identity links a ServiceAccount to an IAM role, so its Pods get AWS keys without storing any.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the file, because it cannot tell what you want to create.
blocks.comment: An identity for Pods, from the core v1 API

blocks.title: Give it a name
blocks.why: The Pod Identity association names it, together with the namespace and the IAM role.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the file, because every object needs a name.
blocks.comment: The name the Pod Identity association refers to
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: aws-caller

blocks.title: A Pod to test it
blocks.what: Three dashes start a second object: a Pod, also called aws-caller.
blocks.why: The Pod shows the credentials EKS gives it.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the file, because every object needs a name.
blocks.comment: A second object: a Pod that uses the identity
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: aws-caller
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: aws-caller

blocks.title: Use the identity
blocks.what: serviceAccountName runs the Pod as aws-caller.
blocks.why: Only Pods using this ServiceAccount get the role’s permissions.
blocks.ifRemoved: The Pod runs as the default ServiceAccount, which has no IAM role.
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: aws-caller
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: aws-caller
spec:
  serviceAccountName: aws-caller

blocks.title: What should run?
blocks.what: A busybox container that sleeps, so you can run commands in it. This block makes the file ready.
blocks.why: busybox can fetch credentials with wget. A real app would use an AWS SDK, which does this for you.
blocks.ifRemoved: Kubernetes rejects the Pod, because it has nothing to run.
blocks.comment: A container to run commands in
blocks.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: aws-caller
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: aws-caller
spec:
  serviceAccountName: aws-caller
  containers:
    - name: shell
      image: busybox:1.37.0
      command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 3600"]

notes.apiVersion: The API group and version. ServiceAccounts and Pods are in the core v1 API.
notes.metadata: Details that identify the object, such as its name.
notes.---: Three dashes separate objects. One file can hold several objects.
notes.ServiceAccount:kind: An identity that Pods run as. Pod Identity links it to an IAM role.
notes.Pod:kind: A Pod runs one or more containers together.
notes.ServiceAccount:metadata.name: aws-caller. The Pod Identity association uses this name.
notes.Pod:metadata.name: The Pod’s name. kubectl exec aws-caller runs commands in it.
notes.spec: What the Pod runs, and as which identity.
notes.spec.serviceAccountName: Run as aws-caller, so EKS gives the Pod the associated role’s credentials.
notes.spec.containers[].name: The container’s name.
notes.spec.containers[].image: A tiny image with basic shell tools, pinned to a version.
notes.spec.containers[].command: Sleep for an hour, so you can run commands in the container.

tryIt.result: Creates an IAM role that only EKS Pod Identity can use. It has no permissions yet.
Links the role to the aws-caller ServiceAccount in default. Put in your cluster name and account ID.
Waits a minute. A new association can take several seconds to work, and EKS adds credentials only as a Pod starts.
Creates the ServiceAccount and the Pod. If the next step shows no AWS variables, delete the Pod and apply again.
Lists AWS_CONTAINER_CREDENTIALS_FULL_URI and AWS_CONTAINER_AUTHORIZATION_TOKEN_FILE, which EKS added.
Prints when the temporary keys expire, and nothing secret. The keys came from EKS, not from the file.
Removes the Pod and the ServiceAccount. It takes up to 30 seconds, because sleep ignores the stop signal.

tryIt.command: aws eks delete-pod-identity-association --cluster-name <cluster> --association-id $(aws eks list-pod-identity-associations --cluster-name <cluster> --namespace default --service-account aws-caller --query 'associations[0].associationId' --output text)

check.run: aws eks delete-pod-identity-association --cluster-name "$LKME_EKS_CLUSTER" --association-id $(aws eks list-pod-identity-associations --cluster-name "$LKME_EKS_CLUSTER" --namespace default --service-account aws-caller --query 'associations[0].associationId' --output text)

tryIt.result: Removes the IAM role. It prints nothing.

questions.question: Where are the AWS keys stored?
answers: In the file, as environment variables
Nowhere: EKS hands out temporary keys to Pods running as aws-caller
questions.explain: The keys are made when needed and expire. No file or Secret holds them.

questions.question: Another Pod in default sets no serviceAccountName. Does it get the role?
answers: Yes, every Pod in the namespace
No, it runs as the default ServiceAccount
questions.explain: The association names one ServiceAccount. Pods running as any other get nothing.

questions.question: What links the ServiceAccount to the IAM role?
answers: A Pod Identity association, made with the AWS CLI or console
questions.explain: Pod Identity keeps the link in EKS, so the file holds no AWS details at all.

fix.message: pods "aws-caller" is forbidden: error looking up service account default/aws-calller: serviceaccount "aws-calller" not found
fix.explain: The Pod names a ServiceAccount that does not exist, so Kubernetes refuses to create it.
fix.fix: Match the ServiceAccount’s name exactly: aws-caller.

sources.title: Learn how EKS Pod Identity grants pods access to AWS services
